blocks.question: netscan shows a TCP connection to 203.0.113.50:443 in state CLOSED, owned by a PID that is in psscan but not in pslist, with an exit time. What does this tell you?
options: Nothing: closed connections are always false positives
The analyst's workstation made the connection
The PID is still running and hidden
A process that has since exited made that connection; its objects survived in memory, so hunt the address and investigate the process's history
blocks.explain: Scanners recover objects that are no longer in use. An exit time means the process ended normally or was killed; the connection and process are still evidence of what happened.

blocks.question: Why might a registry value found in memory differ from the same value in the hive file on disk?
options: The disk version is always encrypted
Changes are held in memory and written to the hive file later, so memory can hold newer values
Registry hives are never loaded into memory
Memory stores only deleted keys
blocks.explain: The loaded hive in kernel memory is the live copy. The file on disk is updated when the system flushes, so recent changes may exist only in RAM.

lessons.title: Credential artefacts: what memory exposes and how to scope it

blocks.md:
The Windows course explained why attackers want LSASS: it keeps credential material for signed-in users so they get single sign-on. For a memory analyst the question is different: **whose credentials were exposed on this machine, and did anyone take them?** The answer decides which passwords to reset and which accounts to watch.

Tiny example: an image from a jump server shows that three admins and one service account had sessions there during the intrusion window. Even before you know whether LSASS was read, those four accounts are in scope for resets.

Where credential material lives in a Windows image, at the level a defender needs:

- **lsass.exe process memory**: material for interactive and cached logons, handled by security packages (the authentication DLLs loaded in LSASS).
- **Registry hives in memory**: SAM (local accounts) and SECURITY (cached domain logons, LSA secrets). Lab 0's hivelist shows both loaded.
- **With Credential Guard**: Microsoft's documentation says the NTLM hashes and Kerberos ticket-granting tickets move into an isolated LSA process, `LSAIso.exe`, protected by virtualization-based security and not accessible to the rest of the operating system. Microsoft also notes what stays exposed: credentials typed for NTLM authentication, and Kerberos service tickets.

Volatility includes plugins that decode some of this material. This course does not cover them: scoping needs to know *that* material was present, not what it was.

Signs in memory that someone took credentials:

- **A handle to lsass.exe with read access.** On clean Lab 0, the processes holding a Process handle to lsass are only System, csrss.exe, wininit.exe and lsass itself. Any other holder with `PROCESS_VM_READ` (0x0010) in its [access mask](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/procthread/process-security-and-access-rights) is a lead. `PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS` includes it.
- **Dump files.** `windows.filescan` lists file objects in memory; a `.dmp` file named after lsass, or created by an unexpected tool, matters.
- **An unexpected DLL in lsass.** Security Support Provider DLLs load into LSASS at start-up and see passwords; adding one is ATT&CK [T1547.005](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547/005/). Lab 0's lsass loads msv1_0, kerberos, wdigest, tspkg, pku2u, schannel and credssp among the 59 modules in its DLL list; compare against a baseline of the same build.
- **Injected code in lsass**: malfind and suspicious_threads results in PID 492 (here) deserve top priority.

blocks.title: Lab 0: who holds a Process handle to lsass.exe (handle count)

scenes.caption: Real windows.handles result on the clean image: four handles from System, one each from csrss and wininit, three from lsass to itself.
Hypothetical compromised host: one extra process (say taskmgr.exe, or a renamed tool) holds a handle with VM_READ. That one bar is the finding.

blocks.md: **Case: Ivanti VPN intrusion, 2023 to 2024.** Volexity reports that after entering through the VPN appliance, the attacker (tracked as UTA0178) used stolen credentials to log into workstations and servers and "dump the memory of the LSASS process to disk using Task Manager", then exfiltrated the output to extract more credentials offline. No attack tool was needed: Task Manager is part of Windows. ATT&CK [T1003.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/) describes LSASS memory dumping in general. Memory captured during or soon after such a dump may show a Task Manager process holding a handle to lsass and a .dmp file object; once Task Manager closes, its handle is gone.

Scope by exposure, not only by proof of theft. Every account with a session or cached logon on a compromised host goes on the reset list. Memory adds who touched LSASS and how, which tells you whether the attacker could also have reached accounts that were not logged on.

blocks.question: Lab 0's baseline shows lsass handles held only by System, csrss, wininit and lsass. In a case image, rundll32.exe holds a Process handle to lsass with access 0x1fffff. Why does that matter?
options: 0x1fffff means the handle is closed
Any handle to lsass is normal
0x1fffff is PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, which includes PROCESS_VM_READ, so rundll32 could read LSASS memory
It means rundll32 is a protected process
blocks.explain: PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS grants every right including VM_READ. An unexpected holder with that access is a direct lead for credential theft.

blocks.question: A host had Credential Guard enabled. Which statement matches Microsoft's documentation?
options: NTLM hashes and Kerberos TGTs are isolated in LSAIso.exe, but credentials typed for NTLM authentication and Kerberos service tickets are not protected
All credentials of every kind are removed from memory
Credential Guard has no effect on LSASS
Credential Guard stores passwords on disk instead of in memory
blocks.explain: Credential Guard narrows exposure; it does not eliminate it. Scope still includes service tickets and anything typed in, so resets and monitoring remain necessary.

lessons.title: Cobalt Strike Beacon in memory: finding and reading its configuration

blocks.md:
The malware course introduced Cobalt Strike, the commercial adversary simulation platform whose implant, Beacon, is widely abused in cracked copies. In an intrusion, a Beacon's **configuration** is the most valuable thing in memory: it names the C2 servers to block, the sleep time and jitter that shaped its traffic, the programs named in its spawn-to settings, and a numeric watermark value.

Tiny example: a malfind hit in a `rundll32.exe` region, a YARA rule for Beacon matches inside it, and a config parser prints `C2Server 203.0.113.50,/updates` and `SleepTime 60000`. You now have a block, a hunt and a timing signature.

How the configuration is stored, as defender tools describe it. SentinelOne's open-source [CobaltStrikeParser](https://github.com/Sentinel-One/CobaltStrikeParser) parses Beacon configurations from PE files, URLs or memory dumps. Its source defines the format: a sequence of settings, each with a 2-byte setting number, a 2-byte type (1 short, 2 int, 3 string or blob), a 2-byte length and the value, all big-endian. The whole block is XORed with one byte: 0x69 for version 3 and 0x2E for version 4. Setting 1 is BeaconType, 2 Port, 3 SleepTime, 5 Jitter, 8 C2Server, 37 Watermark.

Because setting 1 always comes first with type 1 and length 2, an encoded v4 configuration always starts with the same bytes, which is how the parser finds it in a memory dump. It also searches for the decoded start (00 01 00 01 00 02), since a configuration in memory is not always still encoded. Didier Stevens, a security researcher who publishes free analysis tools, maintains another set of blue-team tools, including [1768.py](https://blog.didierstevens.com/programs/cobalt-strike-tools/) for the same job.

blocks.code:
import struct
# Synthetic, defanged blob in the documented Beacon v4 layout:
# entries of (setting id, type, length, value), big-endian, XORed with 0x2e.
SHORT, INT, STR = 1, 2, 3
def entry(sid, typ, val):
    if typ == SHORT: v = struct.pack(">H", val)
    elif typ == INT: v = struct.pack(">I", val)
    else:            v = val.encode().ljust(32, b"\0")
    return struct.pack(">HHH", sid, typ, len(v)) + v
plain = (entry(1, SHORT, 8) + entry(2, SHORT, 443) + entry(3, INT, 60000)
         + entry(5, SHORT, 20) + entry(8, STR, "203.0.113.50,/updates")
         + entry(37, INT, 123456789) + b"\0\0")
blob = bytes(b ^ 0x2E for b in plain)          # what sits in memory
print("in memory:", blob[:12].hex(" "))

NAMES = {1: "BeaconType", 2: "Port", 3: "SleepTime", 5: "Jitter",
         8: "C2Server", 37: "Watermark"}
data, i = bytes(b ^ 0x2E for b in blob), 0     # undo the single-byte XOR
print("decoded:  ", data[:12].hex(" "))
while i + 6 <= len(data):
    sid, typ, ln = struct.unpack(">HHH", data[i:i + 6])
    if sid == 0: break                          # end of the settings
    raw = data[i + 6:i + 6 + ln]
    val = raw.rstrip(b"\0").decode() if typ == STR else int.from_bytes(raw, "big")
    print(f"  {sid:>2} {NAMES.get(sid, '?'):10} {val}")
    i += 6 + ln
blocks.caption: A toy parser on a synthetic, defanged configuration (documentation-only IP, made-up watermark), built with the layout described in CobaltStrikeParser's source. It encodes nothing that runs.

blocks.code:
in memory: 2e 2f 2e 2f 2e 2c 2e 26 2e 2c 2e 2f
decoded:   00 01 00 01 00 02 00 08 00 02 00 01
   1 BeaconType 8
   2 Port       443
   3 SleepTime  60000
   5 Jitter     20
   8 C2Server   203.0.113.50,/updates
  37 Watermark  123456789
blocks.caption: Real output. BeaconType 8 is HTTPS in the parser's table; sleep is in milliseconds; jitter is a percentage.

blocks.title: Decoding the first setting of a v4 configuration

scenes.caption: The bytes as they sit in process memory. The repeating 2e makes them look like noise to a string search.
XOR every byte with 0x2E (v4). 0x2E XOR 0x2E is 0, and 0x2F XOR 0x2E is 1.
Bytes 0 to 1: setting number 1 (BeaconType). Bytes 2 to 3: type 1, a short.
Bytes 4 to 5: length 2. Bytes 6 to 7: the value, 8, which the parser maps to HTTPS. Then the next setting starts.

blocks.md:
Why the configuration is not always readable. Fortra's documentation says the default **sleep mask** obfuscates Beacon in memory while it sleeps, and unmasks it to work. A memory image taken mid-sleep may hold a masked Beacon whose configuration and code do not match signatures. Didier Stevens publishes `cs-analyze-processdump.py` for exactly this case: beacons that use a sleep mask to XOR-encode their writable memory while sleeping.

What still helps: the masking code itself must stay readable to run; the thread that sleeps still has a start address (suspicious_threads); the process still owns its sockets; and network evidence (the regular check-ins from the malware course) points to the PID. Scanning a process's memory with YARA in Volatility uses `windows.vadyarascan`, which needs yara-python or yara-x installed.

Write down what the configuration gives you as response actions: block and hunt the C2 hosts and URIs; search proxy logs for the user agent and the sleep pattern; search other hosts' memory or EDR for the spawn-to programs; and give the watermark and other values to your threat intelligence team to compare across intrusions. A config without actions is trivia.

blocks.question: You find the bytes 2e 2f 2e 2f 2e 2c at the start of a block in a rundll32.exe region. What is the most likely reading?
options: A Cobalt Strike version 4 Beacon configuration: XOR 0x2E gives setting 1, type 1, length 2
A PE header
A Linux ELF file
Random data; config blocks have no fixed start
blocks.explain: Decoded with 0x2E the bytes are 00 01 00 01 00 02: setting 1 (BeaconType), type short, length 2. That fixed start is what parsers search for.

blocks.question: Your YARA rules for Beacon match nothing in an image, but netscan shows rundll32.exe with regular HTTPS connections to a rare host. What fits Fortra's documentation?
options: Beacon never runs in rundll32.exe
YARA cannot read memory images
Sleep masks delete the network objects
The Beacon may have been masked by its sleep mask at capture time, so absence of a match is not absence of Beacon
blocks.explain: The default sleep mask obfuscates Beacon while sleeping. Pivot to the process's threads, sockets and unmasked code, consider a second capture, and use tools built for masked process dumps.

lessons.title: Linux memory: banners, task lists, bash history and kernel checks

blocks.md:
Linux memory analysis follows the same ideas with different structures. Each process (and thread) is a `task_struct`; `linux.pslist` walks the task list starting at the kernel symbol `init_task`, and `linux.psscan` scans for task structures, just like their Windows counterparts.

The hard part is usually symbols. Tiny example from the Volatility 3 Linux tutorial, which uses a CTF image (the "Getdents" challenge from the 2020 teaser CTF of Insomni'hack, a Swiss security conference): the `banners` plugin found **two** different kernel versions in one image, `4.15.0-42-generic` once and `4.15.0-72-generic` four times. Leftover copies of old kernel files can hold banners too. The running kernel's banner is the one the ISF must match exactly.

blocks.code:
$ python3 vol.py -f memory.vmem banners
Offset      Banner
0x141c1390  Linux version 4.15.0-42-generic ... #45-Ubuntu SMP Thu Nov 15 ...
0x63a00160  Linux version 4.15.0-72-generic ... #81-Ubuntu SMP Tue Nov 26 ...

$ python3 vol.py -f memory.vmem linux.boottime
Boot Time  2022-02-10 06:50:16.450008 UTC

$ python3 vol.py -f memory.vmem linux.bash
PID   Process  CommandTime                  Command
1733  bash     2020-01-16 14:00:36.000000   uname -a
1733  bash     2020-01-16 14:00:41.000000   chmod +x meterpreter
1733  bash     2020-01-16 14:00:42.000000   sudo ./meterpreter
blocks.caption: Output shown in the Volatility 3 Linux tutorial for that CTF image, shortened. Meterpreter is the in-memory payload of Metasploit, an open-source penetration testing framework from Rapid7; here it is part of the challenge story.

blocks.md:
Notice two clocks that disagree: bash history times in January 2020, but a boot time in February 2022. The tutorial prints both without comment. When two clocks in one image disagree by two years, find out why before using either: timestamps from memory need the same cross-checking as any others.

`linux.bash` recovers history from the heap of running bash processes, so it can find commands even when the `.bash_history` file was never written or has been deleted.

Other plugins worth knowing, all in the current release:

- `linux.malware.malfind`: mappings that are read-write-execute, executable with no file, or executable with pages written after mapping.
- `linux.lsmod`, `linux.malware.hidden_modules` (carves memory for kernel modules missing from the module list) and `linux.malware.modxview`, which combines them.
- `linux.malware.check_syscall` (system call table hooks), `linux.ebpf` (eBPF, extended Berkeley Packet Filter: small sandboxed programs run in the kernel) and `linux.malware.check_creds` (checks whether any processes share credential structures).

blocks.title: Volexity, Confluence 2022: what memory showed (Linux server)

scenes.caption: Volexity believes one unauthenticated exploit request per server against what became CVE-2022-26134 loads a malicious class into the Java process's memory.
The in-memory implant (BEHINDER) runs commands: the Java process spawns bash, which spawns Python, which spawns an interactive bash.
Volexity had collected memory. Process trees from it showed the web server's unusual children, all running as root.
Heap regions of the Python and bash processes held the typed commands and their output; heap strings about Java classes and methods identified the implant as BEHINDER.

blocks.md: Volexity's write-up describes the method step by step: after spotting the suspicious Python and bash children of the web server, it extracted the memory regions that mapped each process's **heap** (the area for data created at run time). For web servers the heap holds HTTP requests and responses; for shells it holds commands typed by attackers and their output. Volexity then reported the bug to Atlassian on 31 May 2022, and it became CVE-2022-26134. Volexity also noted that the attacker tried to hamper forensic analysis by altering web access logs, yet web requests stored inside the memory samples still helped it rebuild the activity.

Linux images fail more often than Windows ones because of symbols. Before an incident, build or collect ISF files for the kernels you run (the volatility3-symbols project publishes some pre-generated ones), and record `uname -a` at collection so you know which banner to match. The `-u` (`--remote-isf-url`) option lets Volatility search an online ISF index; `--offline` stops all downloads.

blocks.question: The banners plugin shows two different kernel versions in one image. Which one must your ISF match?
options: The first one printed
The banner of the kernel that was actually running, which you confirm from collection notes such as uname -a
The oldest one
Either; Volatility merges them
blocks.explain: Old banners can survive in memory from earlier kernels or cached files. Volatility needs the exact running kernel's banner, so record uname -a when you collect.

blocks.question: Why can linux.bash find commands that are not in the user's .bash_history file?
options: It decrypts the history file
It reads the kernel's audit log
It replays the terminal's keystrokes from the network
It reads history held in the running bash process's heap, which exists before (and even without) bash writing the file
blocks.explain: Bash keeps each shell's history in its own memory. The file on disk is a separate copy that may never have been written, or may have been deleted; memory holds the live one.

lessons.title: Timelines from memory: what carries a time, and merging it

blocks.md:
The prereq course built a super timeline from disk and logs. Memory adds times that disk does not hold: when each running process and thread started, when sockets were created, when a session began, and the system time at capture.

Tiny example: Lab 0's pslist gives cmd.exe a create time of 08:30:18 and DumpIt 08:30:48, both started by explorer. Put next to the disk's Prefetch and event log entries for the same programs, they confirm (or contradict) the disk story to the second.

Sources of time in a Windows image, by plugin:

- **windows.pslist / psscan**: process create and exit times (from EPROCESS).
- **windows.threads / thrdscan**: thread create and exit times; an injected thread created minutes after its process started stands out.
- **windows.netscan**: creation times for many socket objects.
- **windows.sessions**: which user session started each process.
- **windows.registry.userassist**, **windows.shimcachemem**: execution artefacts decoded from the registry and cache in memory.
- **windows.info**: `SystemTime`, the clock at the moment that page was copied.

`timeliner`, per its description, runs all relevant plugins that provide time information and orders the results by time. With `--create-bodyfile` it also writes `volatility.body` (pipe-separated: MD5, name, inode, mode, UID, GID, size, then access, modify, change and creation times) to merge into a disk timeline. In Volatility 3 2.28.2 trust the body file, not the printed table: the table stamps rows with other objects' times.

blocks.title: Lab 0: timeliner rows versus the processes behind them

scenes.caption: pslist on its own: 34 processes with 21 distinct create times, for example cmd.exe at 08:30:18 and DumpIt at 08:30:48.
A full timeliner run (over 14,000 rows) prints 476 PsList rows: in Volatility 3 2.28.2 every row collected so far is printed again after each later plugin, so each process appears 14 times.

Those 476 rows carry only 5 distinct created times, and cmd.exe's 08:30:18 is not one of them: each pass copies one object's times onto every row. Use the deduplicated body file, and check rows against the plugins.

blocks.code:
# Volatility 3: run every time-bearing plugin; -o sets where volatility.body goes
mkdir -p mem_tl
vol -q -f Challenge.raw -o mem_tl timeliner --create-bodyfile > /dev/null

# 2.28.2 writes most body lines many times: drop exact duplicates
sort -u mem_tl/volatility.body > mem.body     # 14,275 lines become 1,424

# The last field is the creation time in Unix seconds
grep -i -E 'cmd.exe|DumpIt' mem.body | head
# |PsList - Process: 2096 cmd.exe (2233099792)|0|0|0|0|0|0|0|0|1540283418

# Then merge mem.body with the disk super timeline from the prereq course
blocks.caption: Run on Lab 0 with Volatility 3 2.28.2. Its timeliner table and CSV copy one object's times onto many rows (see the figure); the body file keeps each object's own times. Rows with identical descriptions merge, so confirm key rows with the plugin itself.

blocks.md:
Rules for memory times:

1. **Know what each time means.** A thread's create time is not the time the code inside it was written there; a socket's creation time is not the time data flowed.
2. **Remember smear** (lesson 4): objects in the image can be younger than its SystemTime.
3. **Convert and record zones**: Volatility prints UTC; check the host's zone and clock offset from collection notes before merging with local-time logs.
4. **Expect gaps**: exited processes may be gone; a timeline from memory covers hours or days of uptime, not months.

Memory gives you the start times of what is running now and a few remnants of what ran before. Disk gives you the long history. The overlap, a process in memory whose start matches a Prefetch run and a 4688 event, is where a timeline becomes solid.

blocks.question: A thread in explorer.exe was created at 10:42, while explorer itself started at 08:05 and malfind flags the region where the thread starts. What does the thread time add?
options: Nothing; thread times are random
It proves explorer was restarted at 10:42
It dates when the injected code started running, which you can match against other events around 10:42
It is the time the image was acquired
blocks.explain: A thread created long after its process began, starting in a flagged region, dates the injection. Look for what happened just before 10:42 on this host and its neighbours.

blocks.question: Why must you deduplicate and filter timeliner output before reading it?
options: Several plugins report the same objects and some report several times per object, so raw rows overstate and repeat events
Because timeliner output is encrypted
Because duplicates mean the image is corrupt
Because body files cannot be sorted
blocks.explain: pslist and psscan both list every process, and in Volatility 3 2.28.2 timeliner also prints earlier rows again after each later plugin: PsList gave 476 rows for 34 processes in a full run, 34 when run alone. Group by object and keep the source plugin.

lessons.title: Anti-forensics against memory analysis, and the cross-view answer

blocks.md:
Attackers who expect memory analysis try to make the image lie. As a defender you need the categories and, for each, the view that still tells the truth. This lesson explains how each trick is caught; it does not explain how to perform any of them.

The general answer is **cross-view analysis**: get the same fact from two places that one change cannot alter together. Tiny example from lesson 6: unlinking a process changes the list, but not the pool allocation, so pslist and psscan disagree. The disagreement is the evidence.

blocks.title: Hiding trick (rows) versus the view that still sees it (columns)

scenes.caption: Each 1 marks a view that still exposes the trick. No single view covers every row, which is why analysts run several.
Unlinking defeats the list walk; the pool scan and the thread scan still find the process (psscan, psxview).

Rewriting the PEB and hollowing fool user-side views; comparing with EPROCESS, VADs, loader lists and thread start addresses exposes them (pebmasquerade, hollowprocesses, ldrmodules, malfind, suspicious_threads).
Hooks are checked against the kernel's own tables and clean system call stubs (ssdt, unhooked_system_calls, check_syscall); a module scan can also find the hiding driver (modscan versus modules).
Sleep masking still leaves threads and sockets in the image; blocked acquisition can only be answered outside it: a hypervisor snapshot, a second capture, network evidence or EDR telemetry.

blocks.md:
The categories, with defender checks:

- **Rootkits** (ATT&CK T1014) hide processes, files, connections and drivers by intercepting or modifying the system's own reporting. Checks: list versus scan for processes (psxview), modules (`windows.modscan` versus `windows.modules`; on Linux `hidden_modules`, `modxview`), and hook checks against the system call table (`windows.ssdt`, which lists the kernel's system call table; `windows.malware.unhooked_system_calls`, which checks ntdll.dll's system call stubs in each process; `linux.malware.check_syscall`) and kernel callbacks (`windows.callbacks`).
- **Masquerading in user space**: edited PEBs, renamed images, DLLs hidden from loader lists. Checks: kernel-side versus user-side comparisons (lessons 7 to 9).
- **Memory-only code that hides between uses**: sleep masking (lesson 12). Checks: threads, sockets, and repeat captures at different times.

- **Interfering with acquisition**: tampering with the APIs or drivers an acquisition tool relies on. WinPmem's answer is three independent reading methods, chosen so that one should work against kernel-mode rootkits. The strongest answer for virtual machines is capturing from the hypervisor, outside the guest's reach.
- **Keeping data out of RAM**: pages that are paged out are not in a raw image. Volatility can combine a page file with the image through a swap layer, so collect the page file too when you can.
- **Destroying the evidence**: attackers who expect analysis also wipe logs, as Volexity saw in the Ivanti case (next lesson). The response is the same as for Duqu 2.0: capture memory early, before restarts and before the attacker knows you are looking.

Note that ATT&CK has moved the log-clearing techniques: Clear Windows Event Logs is now T1685.005 and Clear Linux or Mac System Logs T1685.006.

Every hiding trick must leave the hidden thing working, and working things touch the kernel: they have threads, memory, handles and sockets. Look for the part the attacker could not change without breaking their own code.

blocks.question: A driver appears in windows.modscan but not in windows.modules. What is the most useful interpretation?
options: modscan is always wrong
The driver may have been unloaded or unlinked from the module list; check for an unload record, its memory and any hooks pointing into it
The driver belongs to the analysis machine
It proves the image was taken from a hypervisor
blocks.explain: Like psscan, modscan finds structures regardless of the list. A scan-only driver is either history (unloaded) or hidden; hooks into its memory or callbacks registered by it decide which.

blocks.question: Which capture method gives the best chance against a kernel rootkit that interferes with acquisition inside a virtual machine?
options: Running the same acquisition tool twice inside the guest
Copying the guest's pagefile
Rebooting the guest into safe mode first
Taking the guest's memory from the hypervisor, outside the guest
blocks.explain: The hypervisor holds the guest's RAM and does not depend on the guest's kernel. Rebooting destroys the evidence; inside-guest tools can be interfered with.

lessons.title: Case: Ivanti Connect Secure, and a memory-first workflow

blocks.md:
**Ivanti Connect Secure, December 2023 to January 2024.** In the second week of December 2023, Volexity detected suspicious lateral movement on a customer's network and found webshells being placed on internal and external web servers. It suspected a zero-day but lacked evidence. Working with Ivanti, it obtained **disk and memory images** of the customer's Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) VPN appliance.

Volexity writes that it "analyzed one of the collected memory samples and uncovered the exploit chain used by the attacker": two zero-days chained for unauthenticated remote code execution, CVE-2023-46805 (authentication bypass, CVSS 8.2) and CVE-2024-21887 (command injection, CVSS 9.1). From the memory sample it could recreate proof-of-concept exploits. It published on 10 January 2024 and attributed the activity to UTA0178, which it believed to be a Chinese nation-state-level actor.

Why memory was decisive, from the same report:

- The exploit requests did not appear in the appliance's logs, even with unauthenticated request logging enabled, so "you cannot tell from logs if the server is being exploited."
- In at least one case the attacker cleared logs and disabled further logging.
- The attacker modified legitimate components and added entries meant to evade Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool, and some files run from `/tmp` were no longer on disk.

Volexity combined memory and disk forensics with the Integrity Checker Tool results to find the malicious files, and its advice for a compromised appliance is: do not simply wipe and rebuild; collect logs, snapshots and memory and disk images first, then hunt for lateral movement from the device.

blocks.title: Ivanti case as Volexity reported it (weeks from 4 Dec 2023)

scenes.caption: Second week of December 2023: Volexity's network monitoring sees lateral movement and webshells being placed on web servers.

Volexity and the customer obtain memory and disk images from the VPN appliance through Ivanti. Logs alone could not show the exploit. Bar lengths are approximate: the report gives no dates for these steps.
Analysis of a memory sample reveals the chain of two zero-days. Volexity publishes on 10 January 2024 (week 5), naming both CVEs.

blocks.md:
**A memory-first workflow** that ties the course together:

1. **Collect** before anything restarts: memory with the right tool for the platform (lesson 3), page file if possible, then disk. Hash and log everything.
2. **Identify and verify** the image: `windows.info` or `banners`, symbols, sane process list (lessons 4 and 5).
3. **Processes**: pslist, psscan, psxview, pstree, cmdline; explain every difference and every odd parent (lessons 6 and 7).
4. **Code**: malfind, hollowprocesses, suspicious_threads, ldrmodules; dump and YARA-scan what they flag (lessons 8 and 9).
5. **Connections and objects**: netscan, handles, mutants, registry (lesson 10).
6. **Credentials in scope**: sessions, handles to lsass, dump files, lsass DLLs (lesson 11).
7. **Implant configs** where a family is identified (lesson 12).
8. **Timeline and anti-forensics checks** (lessons 14 and 15), then feed IOCs back into containment and the hunt.

**Practise legally on public training images**, never on systems you do not own or have written permission to examine:

- [MemLabs](https://github.com/stuxnet999/MemLabs): six Windows memory challenges plus a walkthrough (Lab 0, used in this course). Its walkthrough uses Volatility 2; redo it with Volatility 3.
- The [Volatility 3 Linux tutorial](https://volatility3.readthedocs.io/en/latest/getting-started-linux-tutorial.html), which walks through a CTF Linux image.
- [CyberDefenders](https://cyberdefenders.org/) and [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/): blue-team labs that include memory forensics challenges.

Keep a baseline: run every plugin in this course on a clean image of each Windows and Linux build you defend, and save the outputs. Most findings are differences from that baseline.

Memory is where code without files, decrypted configs, live connections and the attacker's last commands live, and it is the first evidence to disappear. Capture it early, verify it, and trust only what two independent views agree on.

blocks.question: In the Ivanti case, why could Volexity not rely on the appliance's logs to confirm exploitation?
options: The appliance had no logging feature
Logs were encrypted by Ivanti
The exploit requests did not appear in the logs even with unauthenticated request logging, and the attacker cleared or disabled logging in at least one case
Volexity had no access to the appliance
blocks.explain: Volexity reports both points. The memory sample, by contrast, held evidence of the exploit chain itself.

blocks.question: A VPN appliance is confirmed compromised. Following Volexity's advice, what comes first?
options: Wipe and rebuild immediately to stop the attacker
Collect logs, a system snapshot, and memory and disk images before wiping or rebuilding, then hunt for lateral movement
Apply the patch and close the case
Reboot the appliance to clear in-memory implants
blocks.explain: Patching and rebuilding do not reveal past compromise, and a reboot destroys memory evidence. Collect first, then contain, then hunt from the device inward.
